passage:
At the district hospital's children's ward, Aditi had one strong first impression of the new nurse, Ishita: late for her first shift, hair still wet, charts left half-filled. In her small notebook Aditi wrote: "Ishita, seems careless. (Guess. Day one.)" Underneath: "What would change my mind? On time for a week. Charts complete. Good with the kids."
Over the next ten days Aditi watched without comment. Ishita came early every day after that first one; her bus route had changed, it turned out. Her charts were tidy. On night shift she sat for an hour with a frightened boy until he slept.
Aditi crossed out "careless" and wrote "rough first day". At tea she said, "I misjudged you at first. Sorry. Want to swap tips on the new chart system?"

qa.q: What did Aditi write in her notebook on day one?
qa.a: "Ishita, seems careless. (Guess. Day one.)"

qa.q: Why did Aditi add 'Guess. Day one.' to her note?
qa.a: She felt cautious about her first impression, knowing it can be wrong, and wanted to remind herself that one late, rushed shift was very little evidence.

qa.q: What made Aditi's approach fair?
qa.a: She wrote down in advance what would change her mind, watched for it quietly, and updated her view when the evidence came.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Aditi apologises at tea?
qa.a: Ishita might feel relieved and welcomed, and more at ease in the new ward. 🙂

grounding: It shows a woman treating her first impression as a guess and looking for evidence that could change her mind.

passage:
Dear Leela didi,
The new flatmate, Rafiq, moved in on Saturday. My first impression, honestly? Loud. He played music till eleven and left a pan in the sink overnight. I caught myself deciding "this will be a nightmare" within an hour.
So I'm trying what you taught me. I've written that impression down as a guess, not a fact. Then I made a list of what would change my mind: does he fix things when asked, does he pay his share on time, how does he treat the cleaning aunty.
It's day five. He turned the music down the moment I asked. He paid the electricity bill early. He talks to Kamla aunty like she's family. The pan is still a problem.
I'm keeping the notebook going. I suspect I'll be wrong in a good way.
Your little sister,
Vinita

qa.q: What did Rafiq do when Vinita asked about the music?
qa.a: He turned the music down the moment she asked.

qa.q: Why did Vinita write her first impression down as a guess?
qa.a: She noticed she'd decided 'this will be a nightmare' within an hour and wanted to stop that quick judgement from hardening into a fact.

qa.q: Why is Vinita's list of what would change her mind useful?
qa.a: It tells her exactly what evidence to watch for, so she can update fairly instead of noticing only things that fit her first view.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel if Vinita had treated her first impression as fact?
qa.a: He might feel judged and unwelcome from day one, even though he turned the music down and paid the bill early.

grounding: It shows a woman holding her first impression of a flatmate lightly and deliberately looking for evidence that could change it.

passage: People ask how I hire. I'm Ankita, I run a small design studio in Kochi, and my amma likes to call me her slow-to-judge daughter. It wasn't always true. Two years ago a candidate called Francis walked in, barely looked up, and mumbled his answers. In the first minute I thought, "Not confident, won't manage clients." Then I remembered I'd been exactly that nervous at my first interview. So I told myself: that's a guess. What would prove it wrong? I asked him to redo one of our old client briefs overnight. The next morning he sent three ideas, clear and clever, with notes a client could understand. On his third day he presented to a client himself. Now I write my first impression on a sticky note and try to disprove it.

qa.q: What task did Ankita give Francis overnight?
qa.a: To redo one of the studio's old client briefs.

qa.q: What made Ankita stop and treat her first thought as a guess?
qa.a: She remembered being just as nervous at her own first interview, so she doubted that mumbling meant he couldn't manage clients.

qa.q: How does the sticky-note habit help Ankita hire fairly?
qa.a: Writing the first impression down and then trying to disprove it makes her look for evidence instead of trusting the first minute.

qa.q: What would have happened to Francis if Ankita had trusted her first impression?
qa.a: He might never have been hired, and the studio would have missed someone who presented to a client on his third day.

grounding: It shows a woman treating a first impression as a guess and testing it with evidence that could change her mind.

passage:
I'm Rehana, and I've taught next door to Zainab for a year at the primary school in Lucknow. I saw how she handled Mr Qureshi.
At the first parent-teacher meeting he stormed in, raised his voice about his son's marks, and walked out before she could answer. The rest of us decided he was a bully. Zainab wrote in her diary, and I saw the line: "First impression: angry, rude. But this is a guess."
Then she did something I didn't. She asked the office when he usually picked up his son. She waited at the gate one evening. She found out he worked nights at the railway yard and had rushed in straight from a shift.
The next month she called him at a time that suited him. He apologised before she said anything.
I still don't know exactly what she was thinking. But she never treated that first meeting as the whole man.

qa.q: Where did Mr Qureshi work?
qa.a: He worked nights at the railway yard.

qa.q: How did Zainab seem to feel about her first impression of Mr Qureshi, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zainab seemed cautious and doubtful about her first impression, writing "But this is a guess" and then finding out he had rushed in straight from a night shift.

qa.q: Which steps by Zainab changed the outcome?
qa.a: Finding out when he picked up his son, talking to him at the gate, and calling at a time that suited him, which gave her new evidence and led to his apology.

qa.q: How might Mr Qureshi have felt when Zainab called at a time that suited him?
qa.a: He may have felt respected and a little embarrassed about the first meeting, which is perhaps why he apologised before she said anything.

grounding: It shows a wise person holding a first impression lightly, noting it is a guess, and looking for evidence that could change her mind.

passage:
Monday: On Shalini's first day at the Shillong newsroom, the new intern corrected Lalremsiami's headline in front of the editor. "It should be 'fewer', not 'less'." Lalremsiami, twenty-five, felt her face burn. That evening she wrote in her notes: "First impression: show-off. Only a guess. What would prove me wrong?"
Wednesday: She asked to see Shalini's first three drafts. They were careful and clear. At lunch she noticed Shalini quietly helping the photographer caption forty pictures before a deadline, asking nothing in return.
Friday: Shalini came to her desk. "I'm sorry about Monday. I was nervous and I blurted it. I should have told you privately."
Lalremsiami crossed out "show-off" in her notes and wrote "careful, nervous, kind". "It was right, though," she said. "Fewer. Want to check my next one?"

qa.q: What did Shalini correct in Lalremsiami's headline?
qa.a: Shalini said it should be 'fewer', not 'less'.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling on Monday, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her face burning, but she wrote her impression down as only a guess and asked herself what would prove her wrong.

qa.q: Which choice helped Lalremsiami change her mind fairly?
qa.a: Looking at Shalini's drafts and watching how Shalini treated others gave real evidence beyond the first awkward moment.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Lalremsiami asks for a check of the next headline?
qa.a: Shalini is likely relieved and pleased, feeling forgiven and trusted after a nervous first day.

grounding: It shows a wise person holding a first impression lightly, noting it as a guess, and deliberately looking for evidence that would change her mind.
